*Śrībodhapañcadaśikā*.
Composed by the great Maheśvara teacher Abhinavaguptapāda. Homage to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
Salutations to the venerable Śāradāmbā.

In this world, indeed, there was the illustrious and great devotee of Maheśvara named Abhinavagupta, an excellent teacher who had reached the further shore of the ocean of the non-dual teaching of Śiva; by virtue of his extraordinary and most acute brilliance, he [was able to penetrate] those things which are difficult to fathom.

Considering the extreme delicacy of certain disciples who were to be graced by the Śaiva Āgamas, [the author], desiring to instruct those who sought to know the tradition of the Trika scriptures without effort, [composed] fifteen [verses].
In order to awaken [the student] to that [truth], he sets forth the meaning of the treatise in verses. Therein, first,
demonstrating that there is no operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the manifestation of the ever-arisen light of consciousness (*saṃvit*), he says:
He whose form is light that never sets, who is both among lights and among darknesses— he alone is within,
and within him are both lights and darknesses.

For the light of the independent Śiva, which illumines all things, is eternally arisen; it does not require another light to illuminate itself because it is self-luminous and because there is no state of non-arising for it. Thus, it is said: "This Self is manifested once and for all. Indeed, this is so.
"Of the seer, there is no loss of seeing, because of its imperishability" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23).

[This refers to] that which is one and without a second, [the witness] of lights such as the sun, as well as of the means of knowledge and so forth, and likewise of states such as intoxication and fainting.

Because darknesses— which are external and devoid of light— reside within [the Self], and because their very life-force is that same light of consciousness which exists externally as well, those lights of the sun and so forth attain their own existence only within that [consciousness].
For no collection of objects, such as a jar or the like, can attain manifestation without the light of consciousness; and those manifestations themselves rise and set.
Furthermore, that light which is unperceived by rising and setting is the root-pramāṇa, the very life-form of all means of knowledge;

no light such as that of the sun or other luminaries is able to illuminate it, because it is itself the object to be illuminated. How could that which is incapable even of self-illumination [illuminate another]?

On the contrary, that which possesses the audacity to illuminate another requires the light of consciousness (*saṃvitprakāśa*) even for its own manifestation; therefore, because it is self-luminous, it alone is the illuminator of the sun and other luminaries. As it has been said:
That which neither the sun, nor the moon, nor even fire can illuminate;
And there is no radiance belonging to the sun, moon, or fire apart from that light.
"Yet there is something innate, but consciousness shines forth in this manner" (Tattvasaṃhitā 3.115).
Likewise, in the Gītā:
"Neither the sun, nor the moon, nor fire illumines that, having gone to which [one does not return]... (Gītā 15.6).
"They return to that supreme abode of mine" (Bhagavad Gītā 11.56).

Even non-cognition, when being made known through cognition, does not differ from it otherwise, because its existence would otherwise be untenable; such is the established position regarding even non-existent things like a sky-flower.
Because it is all-pervasive, the light of consciousness is undivided; it unfolds everywhere as the very self of various diversities, free from obstruction or limitation.
By this it is meant that no means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or the like can serve as anything whatsoever for its life-force. || 1 ||

Thus, having established the relationship between the light of consciousness and that which is to be manifested—the object of knowledge—by the principle that "consciousness manifests the object to be manifested," one might ask: "If this relationship between the illuminator and the illuminated is established, how can there be the state of non-duality with Śiva?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
He alone is the supreme lord, the inherent nature of all beings; for the entire collection of existing things is his very power, consisting of lordship itself.
That very Supreme Lord, whose ultimate reality is the density of autonomous consciousness,
[is the source] of all beings— from Śiva down to the Sakalas—
of the entire class of subjects (pramātṛ), and of both classes of objects of knowledge (prameya).
The nature of the objects of perception and the perceiver, whose essence is the supreme light of vibration, is otherwise— (p.
"Whatever does not find rest therein becomes like a flower in the sky" (Tantrāloka 8.3).

According to this principle, because that which is distinct from the light of consciousness (*saṃvitprakāśa*) lacks existence, nothing at all could manifest. This indeed is the supreme sovereignty of the Lord, an absolute freedom (*svātantrya*) independent of anything else.

Regarding that very manifestation upon the wall of one's own self by its own will alone as the manifold diversity of the universe— which is indeterminate— even there, if it were to assume a fixed form, its sovereignty would be compromised.
As has been stated by the Teacher himself:

If Maheśvara were to abide in a single, unchanging form, he would lose his status as Maheśvara and his nature as pure consciousness, becoming like a jar or other such objects. (Tantrāloka 3.100) This is because on the plane of *māyā*, there exists only the empirical transaction consisting of the relationship between the object of knowledge (*vedya*) and the knower (*vedaka*).
In relation to the imagined subject (*kalpitapramātṛ*), there is a state of being conventionally designated for that specific moment.
As it is said in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:
"It is solely due to the conformity with different objects of cognition, space, and time..."
"The conventional operation of cognition, memory, determination, and so forth is experienced" (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 1.5.21).
However, in reality,
it is always composed of undifferentiated luminosity, having the nature of supreme, ineffable consciousness.

The meaning is that the Supreme Lord alone shines forth through the surging of His own Self as the manifestation of each and every phenomenal entity. Clarifying this very point by way of its cause, he says:
"the entire collection of entities," because it is precisely that Supreme Lord who consists of the nature of sovereignty.

Power (*śakti*), sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), form (*rūpa*), or indeed absolute freedom (*svātantrya*) itself constitutes the multitude of existents consisting of all worldly objects, which are of the nature of both the signified and the signifier; as it has been said in the *Maṅgalā*:

The meaning is that, according to the principle "the entire universe is His power, while the Great Lord (Maheśvara) is the possessor of power," it is indeed absolute freedom (svātantrya) alone that manifests as the self of the universe. As it has been said:
"For consciousness, because its nature is that of the knower, holds within itself various forms."
"It manifests externally at once, both in its universal and particular aspects" (Tantrāloka 1.257).
Likewise, in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:
"For the Lord, whose nature is consciousness, projects outward by the power of His will that which resides within, just as a yogi [does]."
"It shall manifest the multitude of objects without any substrate" (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 1.5.7, p.
And for this reason, Śiva alone, who is replete with his own sovereignty, appears in such and such a manner.
The meaning is that consciousness alone, as the ultimate reality, throbs [with life]. || 2 ||

Now, one might object: "If the universe is thus the power (*śakti*) of the Supreme Lord, then because of the mutual relationship of attribute (*dharma*) and substratum (*dharmin*) between power and its possessor, there is a distinction; how, then, can there be the state of being the single essence of Śiva?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
And power does not desire separation from the nature of the possessor of power;
there is an eternal identity between these two, just as between fire and its capacity to burn. (3)

Just as in the case of fire and its power, because of the inseparable existence (*ayutasiddhatva*) of these two— which possess distinct qualities such as burning, cooking, and illuminating— there is always a state of absolute identity (*aikātmya*), never otherwise.

The burning power and so forth do not attain their own existence without having taken hold of their substrate, fire; according to the principle that "whatever cannot exist without something else is not distinct from it," identity alone is established due to this non-differentiation of nature. As it has been said:
"For when the form of an entity is fashioned by the *mātṛkā* in this or that [context], what real difference is there?
It is like the burning and cooking capacities of fire. (Tantrāloka 1.70).
Thus, the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*) consists in the manifestation of the manifold variety of all phenomenal beings.
One should not seek a distinction between Śiva’s own nature and the characteristic of His power (*śakti*); for if that [power] were to exist as something separate,
its own essential form would be lost, and since the capacity to produce effects is impossible if the essential form is destroyed, this entire universe would not manifest.

And the universe vibrates forth from that; therefore, the very power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*), which is non-different from the light of Śiva, vibrates as the form of both the object of knowledge and the knower.
With this very intention, in the *Śivasūtras*, there is the designation "consciousness is the self" (*caitanyaṃ ātmā*), emphasizing the predominance of the state of being (*bhāva-prādhānyena*).

Nor does the agent differ because of the difference in actions, for even while those actions proceed incessantly, the unity of the agent is not lost. Thus, although there may be a multiplicity of powers, the unity of the possessor of power does not deviate from it, even given that multiplicity.

Since it is included within the single power of sovereignty (*svātantrya-śakti*), that alone is the primary [power]; as that one power is non-different from the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), it is everywhere designated as such. As it has been said:
"Therefore, this very consciousness-nature (*saṃvitti-tva*) is that sovereignty; when it is sufficiently analyzed..."
"It culminates in the powers within the fires" (Tantrāloka 1.61, p.
Likewise—
"His possession of manifold powers is also due to his being inseparable from those very powers" (Tantrāloka 1.68). Likewise:
"This single attribute of His exists by encompassing everything; therefore..."
"It is joined with the power of absolute freedom alone; this is the direct rule" (Tantrāloka 1.67).

This very [consciousness] is defined by such terms as "the heart," "reflection" (*vimarśa*), and "essence" (*sāra*); it is precisely this that establishes the distinction from the light of the insentient. As it has been said:
In the *Pratyabhijñā*:

"They know that the essential nature of manifestation is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); otherwise, even though it is colored by the object, light would be like an insentient thing, such as a crystal. (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 1.5.10)

Thus, because difference, though appearing, is difficult to deny within the path of Māyā and because its essence is mere appearance (ābhāsa), there is no sublation of the non-dual state of the independent Śiva. || 3 ||

Now, one might ask: "With what aim and for what cause does the Supreme Lord engage in the manifestation of the various diversities of the universe? Anticipating this, he says: "That very god Bhairava, whose characteristic is the sustaining of the world, [reflects] everything in the mirror of his own self."
For that which is reflected according to its own capacity. || 4 ||

He alone is the powerful, independent, and unsurpassed Lord (Anuttara-bhaṭṭāraka); because he possesses the nature of sustaining and nourishing the universe— which is manifested through his own sovereignty— by means of its adherence to the wall of his own self, he is Bhairava, whose very essence is the support of the universe.
"By the constant utterance of the word *bhairava*— which means 'he dies,' 'he creates everything,' 'the giver of all,' and 'the pervasive one in the entire universe'— one becomes Śiva.
This is according to the principle stated in the *Vijñānabhairava* (verse 130).

Because [the Self] rests within the nature of Bhairava, which is filled with the wonder of full subjectivity (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*), it is always supported and nourished even by the universe, since it manifests as being identical with the universe; thus it is said to have "the characteristic of supporting the world. This refers to the consciousness of Bhairava.

For, since nothing else exists apart from Him that could be perceived, there is fullness everywhere due to His nature as the sustainer of the universe (*viśvabharita-svabhāva*). It is by the majesty of the density of His own sovereignty that He unfolds Himself in the form of the principles (*tattva*),
elements (*bhūta*), and entities (*bhāva*), beginning with Śiva and ending with the level of Earth.

That very divinity of one who takes delight in the play of concealing His own self should be examined in detail in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* through the exposition of the two words "Turu" and "Bhairava-deva."

(p. 6) This alone is the efficient cause (*nimitta*) for the Supreme Lord at the beginning of the creation of the universe, and not the karma and so forth of living beings; for if He were dependent upon those, His sovereignty (*svātantrya*) [would be lost]. (And yet...)
If [the Lord] were dependent on the karma and other factors of living beings, His sovereignty (*svātantrya*) would be undermined;

yet sovereignty itself is the state of being a mass of bliss (*ānandaghana*). That very [sovereignty], having attained a height of intensity, manifests and shines forth as the manifold variety of the universe through its surging innate nature.

He abides in a state of supreme excellence. As it has been said: "What indeed could one not conceive through his state of absolute sovereignty? And as stated in the *Triśiraḥśāstra*: "He who knows him is a Buddha."

Thus: by its power called "the Supreme" (parā), which— due to its transparency and other qualities— is like a mirror capable of receiving reflections, it [the Self] holds within itself the entire collection of subjects and objects, independently of any causal complex such as material causes and the like.
For a mirror, being dependent upon an external object,
bears within itself the various wonders of its diverse arrangements; this Supreme Power (Parā-Śakti), however, does so entirely independent of such [external objects].
That it manifests the manifold variety of the universe is the play of non-inertness. As Bhaṭṭa Utpaladeva said:
"Salutations to Him who, without any collection of material causes and even without a wall, unfolds the painting of the world."
"To the trident-bearer, who is praiseworthy in his arts" (22.9).
Also, in the *Śrīśaktisūtras*:
"By His own will, He unfolds the universe upon His own screen" (Śaiva Sūtra 2).
Thus [it is said]. The venerable Ācārya also [says]:

"Just as the entire universe shines within itself here, like a variegated arrangement inside a mirror, so too does consciousness, through its union with the essence of its own self-reflection, [manifest] the universe..."
"But the mirror does not touch [the object] in that way" (Tattvasaṅgraha, Āhnika 3, p.
Also, in the *Aṇupratyabhijñā*:
O Lord, without you, the reflection of the entire circle of existence has been shown within your own pure self, just as a multitude of objects is revealed by the power of a mirror or a crystal.

Thus, having raised the objection— “In this way, when the manifestation of manifold forms (*vaiśvarūpya*) occurs, because there is an awareness of duality, how can Bhairava possess non-duality (*advaitatva*)?”—
he says: “This very Supreme Goddess, eager for the awareness of His own nature, [is] fullness...”
In all things, there is for her neither deficiency nor excess.

This power called sovereignty (svātantrya), which manifests as the manifold diversity (vaiśvarūpya) of that very light of consciousness whose nature is Bhairava, is the Goddess because her character is that of play consisting of illumination and so forth; she [resides] within her own self through non-difference from the light.
The Supreme (Parā) shines forth in its fullness through the two acts of perceiving and manifesting the universe;

for within that very state, by perceiving the universe as both the subject and the object— like a city in a mirror— and by reflecting upon it through the differentiation appropriate to the subject of Māyā, [the universe is manifested].
Although she has acquired designations such as "the supreme" or "the non-supreme," because of her sovereignty in the self-reflection of her own nature,
she is eager for the wonder of the universal "I-ness"— the realization that the entire multitude of phenomena is nothing but her own self—
and thus proceeds with intense longing to reflect upon her very self in various ways.

Thus, even in the threefold reflective awareness (*āmarśana*), because there is an absence of orientation toward any externalized entity, it does not depart from its own fullness; rather, by its own sovereignty, it reflects upon itself as its very own self. As it has been said:
In the *Pratyabhijñā*:

"The Lord, having manifested his own self—which is liberated through its sovereignty—by means of volitions such as 'I am Īśvara' and so forth, from that non-dual nature of sovereignty, carries out worldly transaction. (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 1.5.16)
Thus, by this established principle, even when duality manifests, there is no loss of non-duality. For this very reason, she possesses in all things—
every object existing in the universe such as blue, pleasure, and so forth— a complete, undivided fullness (*pāripūrṇya*), which is neither deficient nor excessive.
Because there is no deficiency or excess in the two cognitions of the arising and dissolution of entities,

and because there is no distinction among subjects such as Rudra or the individual soul (kṣetrajña) due to any deficiency or excess in consciousness, its fullness is not lost. As it is said in the *Brahmadarśana*:
That very same consciousness which resides in the sun, the ornament of the expanse of the sky, is the very same consciousness that dwells within the belly of an insect in a hole in the earth.

8) Thus, just as the modes of the spatial regions (*pradeśākāśa*) are not distinct from the great space (*mahākāśa*), so too the manifestations of blue and other objects are not distinct from Brahman, by virtue of its being "great" (*bṛhat*) and its being the "expander" (*bṛṃhaka*).
"Non-occurrence in what is not that [locus]. || 5 ||

For this very reason, the Supreme Lord performs non-differentiated actions, not those consisting of duality; thus he says: "This Lord, eternally eager for the flavor of play with this Goddess, the all-pervasive one, simultaneously effects various acts of creation and withdrawal. (6)

This God of Consciousness, characterized by luminosity and other attributes, having ascended to the plane of recognition (pratyabhijñā), [is united] with this aforementioned Supreme Speech (parāvāk)— who, being of divine nature, possesses the Goddess as her own due to her playful habit of manifesting the universe and so forth.

He is eager for that longing— the *rasa*— for the play consisting of the fivefold acts, which is ever-arisen because it is uninterrupted even during the manifestation of various respective planes, being eternally and incessantly united with the substratum (*dharmī*) of that [play].
Acting there with force and without regard [for anything else], as it has been said:
"Salutation to the Lord, who always sports in creation, who always dwells in the bliss of maintenance, and who is eternally satiated by devouring the three worlds" (Uttara-stotra 22.9).

Thus: "In this way—though incessantly conceptualizing the three worlds with hundreds of mental constructions at every moment, there is a certain one who, though thus conceptualizing, is free from conceptualization; may that Unborn One be victorious! (Siddhāntacintāmaṇi 112).

Thus it is said. And that play is manifold; for instance, in the supreme plane (parā-bhūmi), the state of performing the fivefold cosmic acts is eternally manifest through the uninterrupted manifestation of entities consisting of dense luminosity, as perceived in Paśyantī.
Because of the intensification of the "I-feeling" (ahantā) regarding these manifestations that are about to arise, even there,

by virtue of their being like one's own limbs, the unfolding of the non-projection of duality occurs; and for one who has attained that state, the capacity to perform such functions is exactly of that same nature.

Furthermore, in the intermediate state (*madhyā*), because there is an intensification of the predominance of "this-ness" (*idantā*) within the "I-ness" (*ahantā*) of those entities appearing in an indistinct manner, there occurs an action that is like an indistinct manifestation; however,
at the limit of contraction...

Even within the state of the illusory subject (*māyīya-pramātṛtā*), where one's own self is entirely forgotten, activity remains essentially nothing but differentiation; for even there, since objects such as "blue" have no foundation without the light of the subject, one should fully realize that such activity is itself composed of light (*prakāśamaya*).

Furthermore, since it is proclaimed in the scriptures that liberation from one's own self occurs through the subtle state by means of returning to the attainment of one's true nature (*svarūpalābha*), he says "various" for this very reason.

And it is not the case that, like Brahmā and others, [the Lord] would be able to perform only one of those two [creation or destruction] because his power is restricted and contracted; with this intention, he says "creations and dissolutions" (sṛṣṭisaṃhārān), using the plural number to indicate other functions as well. By this—
He ordains—that is, he performs—the acts of creation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and grace.

He states that there is no restriction here caused by time and so forth by saying "simultaneously" (yugapat), meaning without succession; for in the Supreme Lord, who is not limited by time, such succession does not exist, as He is all-pervasive (vibhu).
The reason for being devoid of spatial and other limitations is precisely this:

therefore, even within these diverse states that occur without succession, the agency of various creations and dissolutions remains uninterrupted. Moreover, this is always the case even with respect to the imagined subject (*kalpitapramātṛ*).

The Supreme Lord, intent on the diversion of creation and so forth, having manifested the circle of the Goddesses of the Senses through the majesty of His own sovereignty, causes the entire range of objects of knowledge to blossom by means of the sport of oscillation, ascending through Sṛṣṭikālī and the others in due succession.
Or, having rested gradually in the abode of Kālasaṅkarṣaṇī,
attain the state of the wonder of the supreme self-reflection of "I," which consists of resting in one's own Self; do this in this very way again and again out of eagerness for the flavor of play.

That he contemplates the performance of manifold creations and so forth is to be understood from his own mouth as something perceivable by those of refined sensibility (*sahṛdaya*). This alone is the identifying mark of Śiva when he has assumed the role of a bound soul (*paśu*), as the venerable Kṣemarāja has said: "Nevertheless..."
In the same way, it performs the fivefold acts; therefore, all this is merely the play of absolute freedom (svātantrya). || 6 ||
Regarding this, he says:
"The fact that He performs what is exceedingly difficult to accomplish is indeed His unsurpassed nature; this alone is His sovereignty, His lordship, and His nature as consciousness. (7)
Thus, for this autonomous Supreme Lord— who is non-dual, abiding as a single unity of light, and who constitutes the universe consisting of the grasped and the grasper—
there exists the state of Sadāśiva, characterized by the presence of "I-ness" (ahantā) in excess of the state of "this-ness" (idantā).
By means of a slight manifestation [of duality] in the Lord, according to the analogy of the two scales of a balance being held equally,

there is the appearance of [the object] outside of itself through absolute differentiation within the impure path— which has difference as its sole life-force— within the principle of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*); yet, even though it has thus appeared, it is again [perceived] non-differently within one's own self.

Immersion in the mass of light— this indeed is the supreme state, even more excellent than the Anāśrita and other levels; this alone is absolute sovereignty (*svātantrya*), this is self-willed freedom (*svācchandyam*) which embraces all powers, wherein all other powers are included.
Because they look toward His face, they are indeed implied by Him;
for this very reason, absolute freedom alone is the primary sovereignty.
By means of the unfolding of the couple (*yāmalaprasara*), beginning with the emergence of unsurpassed bliss (*anuttarānanda*) and so forth up to the point of emission (*visarga*),

one attains the state of *mātṛkā* and *mālinī*, whereby there is a radiant manifestation in a universal form (*vaiśvarūpya*) consisting of various specific signifieds and signifiers. As it has been said:
Therefore, the Lord is unsurpassed because his sovereignty is unsurpassed;
being endowed with the power of emission (visarga-śakti), he is perfected as the one whose form is the universe.

Thus, because that which is not independent lacks sovereignty and is therefore incapable of manifesting the universe, independence alone is the primary cause for the emission of the universe and likewise for the performance of the fivefold acts. As it is said in the *Pratyabhijñā*:
Consciousness, whose nature is self-reflective awareness, arises by its own inherent force as the supreme Word (parāvāk);
this is the primary sovereignty, the supreme lordship of the Self.
"That throbbing, the Great Being, which is undifferentiated by space and time—this very [Being], because it is the essence, is declared to be the Heart of the Supreme Lord" (I.Pra.
1.513). Thus, even its sovereignty is indeed unlimited; for if there were limitation...
Because it would be occupied with only one specific task, like Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or others,
it would indeed lack sovereignty; this very nature of consciousness,
by bringing about a distinction from insentient manifestations, consists of *vimarśa* (reflective awareness).
The nature of consciousness. As it is stated in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*:

"Therefore, the Self is consciousness, the activity of consciousness, and the agency of consciousness; for that reason, its essential meaning has been declared, as it is indeed distinct from the insentient. (*Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā* 1.5.12).
Thus [it is said]. Otherwise, since consciousness devoid of autonomy would—like the *vijñānākala*—be of the nature of non-consciousness, its being overcome by impurity (*mala*) would be unavoidable.
Now, one might ask: what indeed is this "nature of consciousness" that is distinct from non-consciousness? Anticipating this doubt:

Defining the characteristic of the insentient (*jaḍa*), he says: "The characteristic of the insentient is indeed the state of having a delimited manifestation; for consciousness (*bodha*), being distinct from the insentient, is not so measured. (8)
Since insentient manifestation lacks the nature of self-luminosity, it does not possess the capacity even to illuminate itself; what then can be said of its illuminating another?
In that case, because it is utterly mute [regarding consciousness], it is impossible for it to ascend to the nature of cognition.

11) For indeed, an insentient object, distinguished by specific place, time, and form, is delimited by cognition through the exclusion of its counter-correlate; [thus] a jar is [delimited] as being excluded from what is not a jar.

Thus, that which depends on the life-force consisting of the determination of an object preceded by the exclusion of what is not that [object]—this is the definition of the insentient (*jaḍa*). And that [insentience], residing in the cognizer, manifests only by depending upon the living cognizer who thinks "this appears to me"; jars and other such things do not manifest at all [independently].
For them, there is an inherent luminosity; yet because even the constructed subject finds its sole refuge in the insentient, it remains biased toward that side.
Therefore, it is only within the subject consisting of consciousness that the luminosity of the insentient is fully measured.
Establishment [of consciousness] consists precisely in its distinction from that [object], for cognition—

by virtue of not being delimited by specificities such as place and so forth— does not enter the domain of limitation and is thus not measured at all; this is because even the delimiting factors, such as place and so forth, are of the nature of light (*prakāśa*).

Because it is undermined by the dilemma of being either distinct or non-distinct [from consciousness], nor can there be a resting in the self-nature of the "I-consciousness" through an exclusion of what is not that, since there is no other cognizer distinct from consciousness to perform such an exclusion; thus, it would remain a locus for conceptual construction.
Thus, in the passage beginning with "the repose within the light" (*prakāśaviśrānti*), one should understand the distinction from insentient matter (*jaḍa*). As it has been said:
"The I-consciousness (*ahambhāva*) is indeed proclaimed as the repose of the light within itself; and that very [repose] is described..."
Rest arises from the cessation of all dependence.
"Autonomy, agency, and even supreme lordship [are one] (Ajadapramātṛsiddhi 23).
This very thing is the self-luminosity of consciousness:
that while manifesting itself, it manifests the other as well, and by its own autonomy, it renders the other identical to itself.
It manifests through the exertion of the "svāha" ending. || 8 ||
He states that even the manifestations such as emission (*sṛṣṭi*) and so forth, though appearing through His sovereignty, do not have distinct objects:
"In this way, for this Sovereign who differentiates Himself by means of His own powers, emission and withdrawal, which reside within His own Self, exist as His very nature. (9)

Thus, this Supreme Lord, being independent, assumes differentiation through His own freedom— by means of His power (*śakti*) which is non-different from Himself because it is inherent within Him— in the form of the desire to emanate the universe, beginning from Anāśrita-Śiva.

Up to and including the entire class of subjects at the limit [of manifestation], it undergoes differentiation into the categories of the fifteen-fold [tattvas] and so forth, and likewise into the differentiation of objects of knowledge corresponding to those, thereby attaining the distinction between the insentient and the sentient self.
By implication, it is power (*śakti*) itself that, manifesting in the form of the various circles of existence (*bhāva-maṇḍala*),
assumes the state of diverse signifieds and signifiers; the possessor of power (*śaktimān*), however,
because his essence is absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), is one alone, whose primordial nature is unfallen (*acyuta-prācya-svarūpa*), being merely [the source].
When the powers have attained a state of mutual fusion (*lolībhāva*),

through their manifestation, coloring, and so forth, they appear as if divided by difference on the surface; yet, apart from that mere appearance of contraction, there is no other transformation, evolution, or the like.

It is possible [for that]. However, if transformation (*pariṇāma*), manifestation (*vivarta*), and so forth, consist in the appearance of another form or a change into something else, then with respect to the nature of consciousness (*bodhasvabhāva*), the consequence follows that it would be non-luminous (*aprakāśatva*), which is contradictory to it. Even if that consequence were to follow...
Otherwise, because the universe would be like blinding darkness, there would be a total collapse of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

In that case, by embracing such differentiation, [one realizes that] because the Supreme Lord consists of the universe— the essence of which is the wonder of full subjectivity (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*)— all things belonging to the universe [are contained within Him].
Emanation and withdrawal reside within one's own self and are non-different from it;

this is an illustration of the fivefold activities. Because they abide as one with the Light in the state of Śiva, they exist as His very nature, like the limbs of His own body. They are firmly established [therein].

Even at the lower level (*arvāk-pada*), since the creation and so forth performed by Śrīkaṇṭha, Aghora Bhaṭṭāraka, and others do not exist outside the light of consciousness (*saṃvit-prakāśa*), they are indeed identical with it;
thus, even there, the notion of duality does not become an object of experience in the slightest. As it has been said:
Thus [ends the ninth].

Now, having raised the doubt—"In this way, since everything is the manifestation of one's own sovereignty, how does the bondage of individual souls (aṇus) come to be?"—the author states the pair [of verses]:
"Among those [worlds], there is an extreme variety, namely, that which is above, below, and horizontal; these are the worlds."
And its parts are pleasure, pain, and whatever is the notion [of them].
That which is the non-recognition of this [Self] is indeed described as its autonomy; for that very thing which terrifies the deluded is truly saṃsāra. (11)

In those fivefold activities, such as creation and the rest, there is an extreme variety arising from the manifestation of the powers beginning with *apara*, due to the awareness of both difference and non-difference— like a city in a mirror—
and from the awareness of the state of being composed solely of difference; or else, [it arises]...

The diversity of creation and so forth throughout the universe occurs both sequentially and non-sequentially; for while sequence is dependent upon *niyati* (the principle of necessity), there is no fixed order whatsoever for the Supreme Lord, because of His absolute sovereignty and His lack of dependence on the face of the power of *niyati*.

It is expected [by others]. Therefore, the meaning is that He acts by His own will alone, either sequentially or simultaneously. And thus, those objects within the scope of creation and so forth, characterized by various arrangements—whether upward, downward, or horizontal—[are produced].
In the Āgamas, the worlds are briefly enumerated as numbering one hundred and eighteen, beginning from Kālāgni and ending with Anāśrita.
As it is stated in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*:
"In this manner, there are one hundred and eighteen worlds (*bhuvana*) among all the *tattvas*."
It should be understood in brief, but not in detail.
Thus, in detail, the worlds are indeed infinite; and since they consist of many divisions such as cities and so forth, which are portions of those [worlds], likewise,
through the meditations upon the presiding deities of each respective world and so on—

Upon the attainment of various states such as *sālokya* (residing in the same world), when the enjoyment of the corresponding sovereign powers has reached its conclusion for a fixed period, there is the attainment of the station of the Lord of the world above that;
and even there, there is the experience of the bliss of those sovereign powers and so forth.
Furthermore, due to the failure to practice the virtuous conduct taught in the scriptures, one falls into hell;

being overcome by a lack of sovereignty and other such states, one experiences the afflictions of an evil rebirth. Thus, regarding the notions of pleasure and pain within those [rebirths], which arise from the performance of virtuous and non-virtuous actions, there exists therein that which corresponds to the karma.

In that regard, as for "transmigration": it is consciousness alone that, through the excellence of its own sovereign freedom, unfolds the path of space (*deśādhvan*) in the form of a variety of manifestations; therein, it manifests the path of worlds (*bhuvana*), principles (*tattva*), and limited powers (*kalā*), which constitute the objects of expression.
The primary object of expression is the worlds (*bhuvana*), because the categories (*tattva*) and kalās are included within them.

Even the worlds and so forth are not distinct from the Supreme Lord; for if they were so, they would not be manifest, and thus their existence could not be established. Therefore, it is consciousness alone [that is the primary reality].
"In such and such a way it flashes forth externally. As it has been said:
"By means of the variety of forms, this [consciousness] makes manifest the succession of space.
And likewise:
I bow to the manifest form of Bhairava, which has assumed a concrete shape as the solidified flood of the essence of consciousness, appearing in the form of the universe.
Thus it is said:
"In this manner, this entire path is firmly established in pure consciousness alone; for that which does not find rest therein becomes like a flower in the sky" (Tantrāloka 8.3).
And thus [it is said]. || 11 ||
14) That which is the other [aspect] of this world, its parts, and so forth, serving as the indicator for the various paths beginning with the *tattva*s;...
This very consciousness, which is absolute freedom itself, unfolds as the world and so forth;
the non-recognition of this is the perception of bondage, which is contrary to that [recognition] and agitated by suffering and the like. For that indeed...
The capacity to accomplish what is extremely difficult to achieve has been described as "sovereignty" (*svātantrya*).
As it has been said:
"Even though His own nature is unobscured, that which is the self-concealment of the All-pervasive Lord is precisely *māyā*, because..."
Such is the extent of this differentiation that functions throughout the universe. (Tantrāloka 4.11) And likewise, in the *Paramārthasāra*:
"The supreme sovereignty of the Great Lord, which accomplishes the impossible, is the Goddess..."
This power of illusion (māyā-śakti) is the self-concealment of Śiva.
Thus it is said. Indeed, this very cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is for the dull-witted who are deluded by illusion;
it is a source of terror, generating fear of death and other such calamities, like the delusion of a snake in a rope.
This is the intended meaning: just as, through error, one perceives an object that is empty of reality and constructed by conceptualization—

Just as one perceives a terrifying specific form by imagining it to have the appearance of Raudra or other fierce deities, and thereby experiences its harmful causal efficacy, in exactly the same way,
one's own Self, having attained the state of an atom (aṇutā) due to the lack of recognition of its own sovereignty, [experiences limitation].

One is bound by the conceit of caste, stage of life, birth, and so forth; for those who are awakened, having recognized the universe—which consists of their own self—as being both internal and external, are liberated from saṃsāra. And in the absence of that realization, there is nothing [to be gained] except for the play of concealing one's own self, which is not the true reality.

We perceive the cause to be as follows: that very state of Maheśvara’s expanding form, which consists in the concealment of the ultimate reality (paramārtha), is also his very sovereignty (svātantrya). For this creeper of reflective awareness (vimarśa), expanding through the desire to emit the universe, proceeds gradually.
The meaning is that she binds those whose ignorance has blossomed through the nature of the six paths consisting of the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācaka*). As it is said in the *Spanda*:
"This very power, which is of the nature of action, belonging to Śiva and residing in the bound soul (*paśu*), is the binder."
Established in her own path, she is the knower who brings about accomplishment.
Thus [ends the section]. 11.

Now, having raised the doubt as to how the recognition of one's own sovereignty (*svātantrya-pratyabhijñāna*) and detachment from transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) can arise for the limited soul (*aṇu*), he speaks in a pair of verses (p.
Whether it has come from the very essence of His grace, or from the tradition of the Guru, or from the scripture of the Supreme Lord, or from whatever source it may have arrived—(it is so). 12.
That thorough knowledge of reality which comes from the Supreme Lord is liberation; that fullness of the awakened ones is remembered as liberation while living (jīvanmukti). || 13 ||
No austerity, ritual worship, or similar practice is capable of bringing about the recognition of one's own true nature— which consists of the universe yet transcends it—
because such practices belong to *māyā* and are like blinding darkness; only that which is non-*māyic* can reveal the light of consciousness.
Because of the incapacity to manifest [itself];

even if there were a dependence on austerity, dispassion, and so forth for the perception of its own self, another cause would have to be sought for the attainment of those [qualities], and in that case as well...
If there were another cause, it would lead to an infinite regress, and thus [the Lord's] sovereignty would be diminished.
Therefore, the Supreme Lord, desiring to manifest the play of the universe solely by His own will,
conceals Himself by means of His own power called "concealment" (tirodhāna), and then once again...
By that very [grace] called *anugraha*, one recognizes oneself and unwinds [the knots];
and that unwinding, preceded by the clarification of intuitive insight (*pratibhā*) through the power of the supreme descent of grace (*para-śaktipāta*),
is the recognition of one's own self as Śiva, which occurs in many ways due to the variety of the descent of grace.
With the intention that "he becomes [liberated]," he speaks as follows while defining the effects of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*):
"That" refers to someone whose heart has been purified by an intense descent of power,
who [realizes] his own self through a path that is not [dependent on] means (*anupāya*), such as the vision of perfected yoginīs and the consumption of sacrificial pap (*caru*).
"One recognizes" means as it is stated in the *Tantrāloka*:
"The vision of the Siddhas and Yoginīs, the consumption of the sacrificial pap (*caru*), the discourse on the scripture, its transmission, spiritual practice, and service to the Guru."
"O fair-faced one, this is the summary of the methodless [approach], beginning with these words.

For this very reason it is said: "Precisely from the essence of His grace (*tatprasādarasāt*). The word "precisely" (*eva*) excludes any other cause. For grace (*prasāda*), by virtue of the purity of consciousness (*saṃvin-nairmalya*), occurs all at once.
In that state, there is the emergence of the supreme consciousness of Bhairava, because of the absence of repeated practice of means (*upāya*). As it is said in the *Tantrāloka*:
"Śiva does not appear through means; rather, those [means] shine by His grace. He alone is 'I'."
Self-luminous, it shines as the very nature of the universe.
Having heard these words of the Guru once, some become certain; without further investigation, they shine, established as consisting of pure consciousness.

Thus, someone who is graced by the descent of intense *śakti*, having understood the meaning of the scriptures from the mouth of the Guru, attains mastery of the Supreme Reality through the sequence of Śāmbhava means, such as the state of not thinking of anything at all; therefore it is said: "Or [it is attained] solely from the Guru and the scripture."
The meaning is that, by relying on the sequence of awakening taught by the Guru, one contemplates the manifold variety of the universe as a reflection within consciousness. As it has been said:
"In this way, this entire universe is a sufficient reflection within the Lord Bhairava’s sky of consciousness."
"In that which is clear, there is no need for purification by anything else" (Tantrāloka 3.65).

Likewise, a certain person attains recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) through the scripture of the Supreme Lord, aided by right reasoning (*satarka*) and other factors, according to the Śākta method. As it has been said:
"He who possesses this right reasoning (*sattarka*) spontaneously is qualified in all respects; he is consecrated and initiated by the goddesses of his own self-awareness" (Tantrāloka 4.42).
Thus, it is said [that knowledge comes] "either from the scripture or from the Supreme Lord. As for the lower systems (*adharadarśanāni*):
The meaning is: having set aside the teaching of the Supreme Lord, such as the Trika and other systems, and having relied [upon this one]. As it has been said:
"For he considers the entire meaning of the scriptures from *sattarkā* alone; for there is no truth that pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) does not illuminate" (4.44).

Thus, someone possessing a weak descent of power (śaktipāta) may, by means of the sequence of individual means (āṇavopāya) such as vocalization (uccāra), the organs of action (karaṇa), and meditation (dhyāna), ascend the ever-higher steps and attain rest in the state of the Absolute (anuttarapada); therefore, he says:
"From whatever [means] it has come" means that it has arrived or been attained by relying on some coarse means, such as the practice of meditation (*dhyāna*),
by which an immersion (*samāveśa*) arises for them that is constant and free from emergence (*nirvyutthāna*). Thus...

The thorough knowledge of the reality of unsurpassed consciousness— which is the manifestation of one's own sovereignty through the unfolding of the wonder of the "I-consciousness" that is completely full of the universe— is itself liberation, and not anything else.
It is the attainment of another location delimited by [the realms of] the gods and so forth. As the Teacher said (p.
"For liberation there is no abode whatsoever, nor is there going elsewhere."
"Liberation is the piercing of the knot of ignorance and the manifestation of one's own power" (Pañcārthabhāṣya 60).

This very state of being the Supreme Lord is the nature of the Lord’s sovereignty (*pārameśvaryam*), which consists of the radiance of that very universe in its various forms; it is composed of undivided light, and not the powers of *aṇimā* and other [superhuman] attainments (*siddhi*) which consist of duality.
This very state is the fullness of the awakened ones, who possess a consciousness consisting of the reflective awareness of perfect I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhantā-vimarśa*);

it is their nature of being filled with the universe. That same state is liberation for those subjects who, while maintaining the body, vital breath, and so forth, remain alive; it is the state of being a Śiva while living (*jīvacchivāvasthā*).
It is recorded thus in the treatises. || 12-13 ||

Thus, he states that even the conceptualization of bondage and liberation is merely imagined: "Both this bondage and liberation do not differ from the nature of the Supreme Lord; for in reality, there is no duality in the Supreme Lord. (14)
These two— bondage and liberation, characterized as just described—
do not differ from the nature of the Supreme Lord because they are fashioned by His mere will; due to the sovereignty of consciousness, they do not exist as something separate.
The meaning is that, if they were distinct from that [consciousness], they would not manifest because they would not be perceived.

For, out of his own will— being one who delights in the sport of concealing his own nature— the Great Lord, with the intention of displaying the drama of the universe, [acts] upon the stage of the inner self.

The actual meaning is this: by assuming various mental states (*bhūmikās*) manifested through determinants (*vibhāvas*), consequents (*anubhāvas*), and so forth, accompanied by involuntary emotions (*sāttvikabhāvas*) and other factors, one relishes the aesthetic wonder (*camatkṛti*) of the pure, supramundane *rasa* that has been fully unfolded by those respective permanent moods (*sthāyibhāvas*).
Due to the absence of higher knowledge, those whose supreme reality has been stolen away by other powers develop the conceit of bondage; however, for those who are vessels of grace,
there is only the sovereignty of the mass of consciousness (*ciddhana*) manifesting as the internal and external universe.

For those who possess the higher knowledge that "it throbs," there arises the conceit of liberation for those who have attained the treasure of the supreme reality, as the Lord reveals the universe— which is non-different from Himself and consists of pure light— by means of the wheel of powers (śakticakra) whose nature is not terrible. Thus, both of these [the attainment of the treasure and the conceit of liberation] belong to the Blessed One.
It unfolds by its own free will; therefore, because it consists of that power, the intended meaning is that this is not different from it—this he confirms with a statement of reason:
"for there is no difference," since in reality, in the ultimate sense, there is no difference within the Self, the Supreme Lord.

Since everything has as its ultimate reality the essence of light, even the slightest trace of the conceptualization of difference is impossible; therefore, through the intensification of the wonder of the full sense of "I," the full unfolds within the full, and there is no such thing as an "incomplete" state consisting of the conceptualization of bondage, liberation, and so forth.
Everything is irreproachable.
As it has been said:

In reality, there is no saṃsāra for embodied beings; what talk can there be of bondage? For one who is never bound, the act of liberation is futile. This delusion of sorrow caused by false ignorance is like the error of mistaking a rope for a snake or a shadow for a thief—do not abandon anything, do not grasp at anything; simply wander.
Established in his own nature, he remains as he truly is.
Thus [ends the section]. || 14 ||

Thus, he states the means for attaining that meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) which is filled with the savor of supreme lordship and provides consolation even during the state of being alive, for those who possess direct knowledge of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*):
Thus, Bhairava—the essential nature of all existents—is contemplated as resting upon the lotus of the trident of the powers of will, knowledge, and action. 15.
By means of this aforementioned reflective awareness (*parāmarśana*), the nature of all entities— whether internal or external,
such as blue, pleasure, and so forth— is Bhairava, whose essence is light;
because his nature fills the universe, he is the full, autonomous light of Śiva.

It is thoroughly investigated and reflected upon: that within one's own self, in the sky of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), while manifesting the universe, the creative subject is the "all-pervading self" (*viśvātmaka*);
thus, by the expression "the nature of Bhairava," it is indeed the consciousness of Bhairava itself.
Whatever manifests externally or internally as this or that state, all of it is illumined by the sovereign powers of the senses; it is one's own Self alone that,
through its absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), perceives itself within itself, and not anything separate— this is what was stated.
In the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:
"For the Immeasurable One, however, all objects appear as full within His own Self by means of His own Self.
To the question "Of what nature [is He]?", he says: "Will," "Energy," and "Action" refer to the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).
The three powers of will, knowledge, and action constitute the trident due to their equality as spokes;

therein resides the lotus, well-known from the *Matsyodarīmata* and other sources, which possesses the qualities of contraction and expansion. That [lotus] is the state of the Transmental (*maunasa*), and [the subject] appears as resting upon it while simultaneously manifesting as transcending it.
This is the meaning (p.
furthermore, [it refers to] the existence of the universe as not being distinct from the light of consciousness.
To demonstrate this, the arising of even the seed-syllable of Śrīparā has been proclaimed; therein, by the word "svabhāva," the extraction of the nectar-seed (amṛtabīja) is performed.
Since that [seed] is without vowels (anacka), its pronunciation is impossible; therefore, in this fourteenth abode—

By the statement "in which the three powers have become manifest," the extraction of the seed-syllable of the trident (*śūlabīja*) is indicated by the term *icchākalā*. By the phrase "Bhairava, because his nature consists of filling and vomiting," the extraction of the emission (*visarga*) is shown in its twofold form as both external and internal.

By the phrase "of all existents" (*sarvabhāvānām*), its pervasion is stated. As it is said in the *Mālinīvijaya*: "The three cosmic eggs are pervaded by the letter *sa*; the fourth by the trident; that which transcends all is pervaded by the emission (*visarga*); this is held to be the pervasion of Parā."
Thus it is said:
"For this very reality, rooted in Brahman and known as the Egg of Māyā,
cannot be called 'existent' at all without the ascent of will, knowledge, and action."
Indeed, through the ascent of those three powers within the Bhairavian sky of consciousness, that [object] is either emitted externally or it is emitted [internally].
And thus: when the seed-syllable of Parā, which possesses such pervasion, is practiced without interruption, the attainment of sovereignty occurs through immersion into the Supreme Lord;
for by means of the glance of the instrument [of consciousness], there arises the reflective awareness of this seed-syllable, which is the cause of all accomplishments.
The Teacher has indicated this by way of illustration. || 15 ||
Now the Teacher concludes by mentioning his own name and turning [the reader] toward the meaning of the treatise:
"These [verses] were composed by Abhinavagupta in order to awaken students of tender intellect easily."
Fifteen verses have been declared. || 16 ||
Thus ends the Bodhapañcadaśikā.
Those of delicate intellects, possessing a mild descent of power, [attain it] effortlessly; the rest is clear.
The venerable Abhinavagupta, whose name is praised as Māheśvara, composed this most delightful *Bodhapañcadaśikā* for the instruction of those possessed of dull intellect; therein,
Harabhaṭṭa Śāstrī has composed this commentary.
In the year 4990 of the Bhūnanda-nanda-Veda era, on the eleventh lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna in the Laukika calendar, Śāstrī Hara composed this commentary.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Bodhapañcadaśikā*, composed by the illustrious Abhinavagupta, the preeminent teacher of the Great Māheśvaras, as prepared by Paṇḍita Harabhaṭṭa Śāstrī.
May there be dedication to Śrī Śiva.
